1.pericope_label: In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him), and fought against Ashdod, and took it... At the same time spake the LORD by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, Go and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins

schools.summary: Ellicott answers the identity of Sargon from the monuments: before their discovery the name appeared nowhere but in this verse and his very existence had been questioned, whereas he now stands out as one of the greatest Assyrian monarchs, who succeeded the conqueror of Samaria first as co-regent and then in his own name until Sennacherib followed. He also makes the general's name an official title, that of the commander-in-chief next in authority to the king, dates the campaign from the annals in which an Ashdod king refused tribute and was deposed for his brother, holds that month by month for three whole years the prophet was seen in the streets as one already a prisoner of war, and confines the nakedness to laying aside the rough outer robe the prophets habitually wore. Delitzsch presses the identification further, that Sargon and not his predecessor took Samaria after a three years' siege and boasted of carrying away the house of Omri, that the predecessor died before the city while Sargon seized the throne after a contest with the lawful heirs, and that he was therefore a usurper.

Gill takes the general's name for a personal name rather than a title, gives the Greek and Arabic forms of it, and makes its bearer one of Sennacherib's generals. Calvin argues that Sargon must be Sennacherib, since the general named here was one of Sennacherib's captains, which constrains us to acknowledge that this king had two names; and he draws a rule from the prophet's nakedness, that had it been done of his own accord he would have been justly ridiculed, but done at God's command it can only excite awe, and that since God never acts without explaining his reason the prophet states the design as well as walking. False prophets imitate the practice, putting on varied and imposing shapes to dazzle the eyes of the multitude, but their symbols are worthless because God is not their author, which he makes the rule for meeting those who offer empty ceremonies in place of true sacraments.

Clarke identifies Sargon with Sennacherib, possibly under one of the seven names an early father says he bore, notes two further names given him in the Apocrypha, and adds that Ashdod was a strong town which held out twenty-nine years against an Egyptian king long afterwards. On the sign he thinks it improbable that the prophet walked uncovered three years, since three whole years of it could give no premonition of the time, whereas three days would, a day standing for a year by the prophetic rule; he suggests either that the words for three days dropped out of the text after barefoot or that a Greek translator read years for days. Wesley equates Sargon with Sennacherib and explains the nakedness as going without the upper garment as slaves and prisoners went, and barefoot as mourners and captives did.

Henry leaves the identification open between Sennacherib and his predecessor, dates the prophecy by the siege itself, an event so remarkable that those living then could fix the year by it, and notes that the prophet had already been a sign in the sackcloth he had long worn, which some take him to have put on when the ten tribes were carried away and others to have been his ordinary dress.

debates.question: Is Sargon another name for Sennacherib?

positions.view: Yes; the general named here was Sennacherib's captain, and the king bore several names.
Open: some take him for Sennacherib, others for his immediate predecessor.
No; the inscriptions show a distinct and major king, whose existence was doubted before they were read.
No; Sargon took Samaria himself and usurped the throne after his predecessor died before the city, so the old identification cannot stand.

debates.question: How long did the prophet go stripped?

positions.view: Probably three days, standing for three years; three years of it would have signified no term at all, and the text may have lost the word for days.
Three whole years, month by month in the streets, with no adequate grounds for shortening it.

outliers.note: Proposes that the words for three days have dropped out of the Hebrew text, or that a Greek translator misread days as years, rather than accepting the received term.
Turns the prophet's nakedness into a test for distinguishing God-given signs from invented ceremonies, and applies it against the sacramental practice of his opponents.

themes: In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it;
At the same time spake the Lord by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, Go and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins, and put off thy shoe from thy foot. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot.

3.pericope_label: And the LORD said, Like as my servant Isaiah hath walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia... And the inhabitant of this isle shall say in that day, Behold, such is our expectation, whither we flee for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria: and how shall we escape?

schools.summary: Ellicott holds that the sign was made in act and in silence, its meaning left unfolded until the three years ran out, and notes that Egypt and Ethiopia stand connected here as in the two preceding chapters, both being under a king of Ethiopian stock. He observes that the prediction was fulfilled under neither Sargon nor Sennacherib but under a later king who subdued the whole of Egypt and set satraps over its provinces, that the prophet paints the brutality of a prisoners' march in vivid colours, and that two outside witnesses confirm the picture, the Assyrian officer's scornful phrase about a bruised reed and a later prophet's mention of Thebes as already conquered; he renders the closing word coast-land and refers it to the whole seaboard, Philistia foremost in the revolt with Phoenicia and perhaps Cyprus. Delitzsch puts the question the passage turns on, what impression the humbling of Egypt and Ethiopia would make on those who leaned upon a power supposed unapproachable and invincible, and renders their cry as a discovery of having been deceived by the nation they looked to and the nation they gloried in.

Gill notes that the explanation of the sign now follows, has those who trusted these nations afraid their turn is next and ashamed of having trusted at all, and follows the rabbis in taking the isle for the land of Israel, which bordered the sea and was in any case cut off from other countries, reporting also the opinion that Jerusalem is meant and that the word means simply a region, watered or not. Calvin gives the reason for the three years, that it was the truce granted those nations for repentance and a trial of the obedience of God's own people, and that the spectacle exposed the rebellion of the wicked who displayed their impiety in despising the prophet's nakedness while the godly looked past it to the mark the Lord had set upon it; he states for whose benefit the oracle about foreigners was given, that the Jews might learn in their afflictions to hope in God rather than have recourse to forbidden aid; and he extends the closing name to the whole of Judea, doubting the usual reason drawn from the Mediterranean shore, remarking that in Hebrew to look often means to hope, and warning that if we refuse the sure refuge God offers we shall deservedly lie down naked and destitute.

Wesley says the term of the sign was not served constantly but only when the prophet went abroad among the people for whom it was appointed, notes that the captives' garments were cut off by the middle, agrees that although the words are general the Israelites are principally intended, and closes with the confession the last verse puts in their mouth, that so vain is a hope placed on a people unable to deliver themselves.

debates.question: Who is the inhabitant of the isle that speaks at the close?

positions.view: Israel, the land bordering the sea and cut off from other countries; or, on another opinion, Jerusalem.
The whole Philistine and Phoenician seaboard, perhaps including Cyprus.
The whole of Judea, not Jerusalem only, and not for the reason usually given from its Mediterranean shore.
The land the prophet was in, whose inhabitants the words were addressed to.

debates.question: Why was the sign given for three years?

positions.view: As a truce for the doomed nations to repent, and a trial of God's own people's obedience.
Because the sign was made in act and in silence, its meaning withheld until the term expired.
To date the judgment three years from the prophecy, the term being served only when the prophet went out among the people.

outliers.note: Concedes that the prediction was fulfilled under neither of the kings named in the chapter but only under a later Assyrian who conquered Egypt outright.

themes: And the Lord said, Like as my servant Isaiah hath walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia;
So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives, young and old, naked and barefoot, even with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt.
And they shall be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory.
And the inhabitant of this isle shall say in that day, Behold, such is our expectation, whither we flee for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria: and how shall we escape?
